caption:
Were the Altamira cave paintings a forgery?

Experts said yes for over twenty years. Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola published them in 1880 as Paleolithic work; at the Lisbon Prehistorical Congress that same year his findings were ridiculed. French specialists led by Gabriel de Mortillet and Émile Cartailhac argued prehistoric people lacked the ability for abstract thought. A fellow Spaniard claimed a living artist had painted the ceiling on Sautuola's orders.

The case against him was soot. He could not explain why the walls bore no smoke marks. He later worked out that a lamp burning marrow fat produces far less soot than other fuels.

A rockfall had sealed the cave about 13,000 years ago. A local tiler, Modesto Cubillas, found it in 1868 after a falling tree disturbed the rocks. In 1879 Sautuola's eight-year-old daughter María led him inside, and he realised the markings were drawings.

By 1902 similar paintings had accumulated across the Franco-Cantabrian region and the evidence could no longer be rejected. Cartailhac published his retraction, "Mea culpa d'un sceptique". Sautuola had died fourteen years earlier.

Still open: the age. There is no scientific agreement on dating. Uranium-thorium work put a large red claviform sign at about 36,000 years and a dotted horse in the same chamber at about 22,000 — more than 10,000 years of painting.

The cave is shut. Visitors' breath damaged the art, it closed in 1977, and green mould appeared in 2002.

Images: Cartailhac's 1906 tracing, an early drawing of the ceiling, two 1912 Illustrated London News pages, and a replica ceiling in Brno. All public domain.
